q: my 2 year old has a fever of 102.5, should I give Tylenol?
text:
102.5 °F = 39.2 °C.

Yes, you can give acetaminophen (Tylenol) — it helps reduce fever in children, according to MedlinePlus [4]. Give it every 4 to 6 hours, and know your child's weight before giving it [4].

The main goal is your child's comfort, not bringing the temperature to normal, according to the SEUP [3]. Offer plenty of fluids, keep the room at a neutral temperature, and don't overdress them [3]. It's normal for them to have no appetite — don't force food, but keep offering liquids [3]. You can give either paracetamol or ibuprofen if they're distressed or uncomfortable [2]. Never give aspirin to a child [4].

Get medical advice if:
- The fever lasts 5 days or more [7]
- They have a rash along with the fever [7]
- They're not eating or not themselves, and you're worried [7]
- They seem dehydrated — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [7]
- They're drowsy and hard to wake, or breathing fast [7]

q: my baby is 7 months and has been warm since last night, 101.8 F
text:
A fever is a sign the body is fighting an infection, and most often it lasts two to four days, according to the SEUP [2]. A temperature of 101.8 °F is a fever, and the aim of treatment is to ease the discomfort it causes, not always to bring it down to normal [4].

You can give paracetamol or ibuprofen for the discomfort; paracetamol is the first choice, and the dose depends on your child's weight [4]. PediBot's dose calculator can help you work out the right amount. Keep offering fluids to prevent dehydration [1]. Do not give aspirin to a child with fever [1].

Get help if your child:
- is listless, barely responsive or very irritable [7]
- has trouble breathing [7]
- has spots that do not fade when pressed [7]
- will not take solids or liquids by mouth [7]

Also watch their general condition and colour at home [2].

q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text:
Yes — ibuprofen (Motrin) can be given to a child over 6 months old for fever, according to MedlinePlus [6]. Give it every 6 to 8 hours, and check the packaging or leaflet to be sure it suits your child [2][6]. Know your child's weight before giving it [6].

Do not give ibuprofen if your child is under 3 months, weighs under 5kg, has chickenpox, is dehydrated, or has asthma unless a doctor recommends it [1]. Do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to [1].

Also give plenty of fluids, keep breastfeeding as normal, and check on your child regularly, including at night [2].

Get medical advice if:
- Your child is not their usual self or not eating [1]
- Signs of dehydration — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [1]
- The fever lasts 5 days or more [1]
- The medicine is not helping [2]

q: my 4 year old has had fever for 3 days but is still playing
text:
A fever is very common in young children and usually settles within 1 to 4 days, according to the NHS [2]. It is the body's normal response to fighting an infection, and it is not a sign of seriousness by itself [4].

Keep them comfortable and well hydrated: offer plenty of fluids, keep the room at a neutral temperature and ventilated, and avoid wrapping them in too many clothes or blankets [6]. It is normal for them not to want to eat — do not force them [6]. If they are uncomfortable, paracetamol or ibuprofen can be given at the dose your pediatrician recommends, every 6 to 8 hours; do not alternate them routinely every 3 to 4 hours [6]. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [1]. Do not sponge them down or use cold water to cool them [1][6].

Get help if your child:
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [1]
- is not their usual self, or you are worried [1]
- is dehydrated — diapers not very wet, sunken eyes, no tears when crying [1]
- has a rash, or a stiff neck, or is bothered by light [1]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or has difficulty breathing [1]

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text:
Vomiting twice in a morning is often the start of a stomach bug, and the main risk is dehydration, according to the SEUP [1]. What matters most is getting fluids back in.

Wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution — 2 to 5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour [3]. Watch how well he takes it; if he keeps it down, you can slowly give it more often [3]. Don't use homemade drinks like lemonade or commercial soft drinks [3]. You can buy oral rehydration solution for children without a prescription [5].

Get help if:
- He is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [7]
- He vomits a lot, can't keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without drinking [7]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [7]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or urinates little [7]
- He has severe belly pain or a headache [7]

q: my 3 year old keeps vomiting every time he drinks water
text:
Vomiting that happens every time he drinks is a sign he is not keeping fluids down, and the aim is to get small amounts in often rather than a full glass. Offer small sips of water, or let him suck on ice chips, according to MedlinePlus [1]. The NHS adds that small sips of rehydration solution replace lost fluids well — ask your pharmacist to recommend one — and that you should keep giving his usual diet in small amounts [3]. Do not give fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make vomiting worse [3][5].

Get help if:
- He vomits a lot, cannot keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even when he takes nothing [2]
- The vomit is green, contains blood, or looks like coffee grounds [2]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or passes little urine [2]
- He has severe tummy pain or a headache [2]

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the causes [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, according to the SEUP [3].

Give fluids as oral rehydration solution, which you can get over the counter — it is the most helpful for mild dehydration [2][4]. After your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give 2–5 ml of oral rehydration solution every 5 minutes for an hour [5]. If they keep it down, you can slowly increase how often you give it [5]. Do not use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks [5].

Get help if:
- Your child is very drowsy or floppy [3]
- They vomit many times or refuse all fluids [3]
- They vomit even when they have taken nothing [6]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [6]
- You think they are severely dehydrated [2]

q: my daughter has diarrhea since yesterday and doesnt want much food
text:
Diarrhea in children is usually caused by a virus and gets better on its own with rest and plenty of fluids, according to MedlinePlus [2][4]. Rotavirus is the most common cause of acute diarrhea in children [4].

Offer fluids and electrolytes often, in small sips, and let her eat what she wants — she does not need to eat much while she is unwell [2]. Your provider may suggest a probiotic, as some may help shorten a case of diarrhea [2].

Contact a provider right away if she has any of these:
- Change in mental state, such as irritability or lack of energy [3]
- Diarrhea lasting more than a day [3]
- Any fever in infants, or high fever in older children [3]
- Vomiting often [3]
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual or no wet diapers for 3 hours or more, no tears when crying [3]
- Stools that are black and tarry or contain blood or pus [3]

q: can I give Pedialyte after every loose stool
text:
Yes — children with diarrhoea should be given an oral rehydration solution to replace the fluids and electrolytes they lose, according to MedlinePlus [2]. The SEUP says to offer it in small amounts [3], and the WHO says oral rehydration solution is a mix of clean water, salt and sugar that is absorbed in the small intestine and replaces the water and electrolytes lost in the stools [4]. Do not use homemade solutions or commercial soft drinks to replace these losses [3]. Keep feeding: continue nutritious food, including breast milk, during the episode [4].

Get help if:
- Much thirst, crying without tears, little urine or sunken eyes [3]
- Marked irritability, drowsiness or reduced responsiveness [3]
- Stools so watery and frequent that the child cannot drink fast enough [3]
- Refusing to eat or drink [3]
- Persistent or intense belly pain, or stools with a lot of blood [3]

text:
Watery poop without blood is usually gastroenteritis, an infection of the gut that is not usually serious but can cause dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [5]. Offer plenty of fluids in small, frequent sips, and keep breastfeeding or formula-feeding as normal [2][5].

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do
text:
A cough that keeps a child awake at night is common with colds and usually settles on its own, according to MedlinePlus [6]. There is no cure for a cold, but you can help your child feel better while it passes: let them rest, offer plenty of fluids, and run a clean humidifier or cool-mist vaporiser in the room [6]. Saline nose drops or sprays can also help [6]. Do not give aspirin to children or teenagers, and ask your doctor or pharmacist before giving any over-the-counter cough or cold medicine, since some contain ingredients not recommended for children [6].

Get medical help if your child has:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [6]
- Signs of dehydration [6]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [6]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days with no improvement [6]
- Symptoms that improve, then come back or get worse [6]

q: my baby has a cough and sounds very congested when sleeping
text:
A cough and a blocked, noisy nose are very common in babies, and most of the time they are not serious. The safest place for your baby to sleep is in a separate cot or Moses basket that is free from toys, blankets and pillows, according to the NHS [3].

To help with the congestion, keep your baby's cot clear and let them sleep on their back on a firm, flat mattress [1]. If you share a bed, keep pillows, sheets and blankets away from your baby, and do not swaddle them [1].

Get help if:
- Your baby is struggling for breath [7]
- Your baby stops breathing or will not wake up [7]
- Your baby's lips, tongue, face or skin turn pale, blue or grey [7]
- Your baby is limp, floppy or not responding as usual [7]
- You are worried about your baby or think they might be ill [7]

q: my 3 year old has a barking cough but is breathing okay
text:
A barking cough that sounds like a seal, with a hoarse voice, is the usual sign of croup, according to the NHS [1]. It often starts like a cold and is usually worse at night [1]. Most cases are mild and get better in a few days, though the cough can last up to a week, according to the SEUP [3].

Offer fluids if there is fever and give the usual fever medicine [3]. Do not put your child in a steamy room or have them breathe in steam [7]. Cough syrups and cough suppositories should not be given without checking with your paediatrician [4].

Get help if:
- Noisy breathing when breathing in, even at rest [4]
- Breathing gets faster, ribs pull in, or chest sucks in [4]
- Trouble swallowing or lots of drooling [4]
- Struggling to breathe, or blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue [7]
- Sleepier than normal, difficult to wake, or limp and not responding [7]

q: my son has been coughing for a week after a cold
text:
A cough after a cold can last a while: cold symptoms can last 10 to 14 days, according to MedlinePlus [6]. If the cough has changed into a barking cough that sounds like a seal, with a hoarse voice or a rasping sound when breathing in, that points to croup, according to the NHS [2]. Croup symptoms usually come on after a few days and are often worse at night [2].

What to do now: keep the room comfortable and avoid steam — do not put your child in a steamy room or have them inhale steam [7]. Offer fluids often and let them rest.

Get help if:
- They are struggling to breathe, with grunting or their tummy sucking under the ribs [7]
- Their skin, lips or tongue look blue, grey, pale or blotchy [7]
- They are sleepier than normal or hard to wake [7]
- They are limp, floppy or not responding as usual [7]
- They are very upset or restless and cannot be calmed [7]

If the cough is getting worse or not getting better, ask your doctor — they may give medicine to shorten the illness [2].

q: these spots dont seem to bother her but there are more every morning
text:
The spots you describe — not itchy, and more of them each morning — are not something the sources describe as a single condition, so I can only tell you what they do cover.

Scabies causes intense itching, often worse at night, with bumps and lines on the fingers, wrists, arms, legs and around the waist, according to the WHO [1]. In babies and small children the rash can be more severe, especially on the palms, soles and scalp [1]. Itching is the main symptom, so a rash that does not bother her does not fit that picture [1].

Measles causes a red, blotchy rash that usually starts on the head and spreads down the body, with fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes [2][3]. A rash alone, without those, is not described that way [2][3].

See your doctor if your child has:
- A rash or skin infection [6]
- Fever above 102°F (38.8°C (101.8 °F)) [6]
- Weight loss or a big change in weight [6]
- Trouble sleeping or behaviour changes [6]
- Frequent sore throats or breathing problems [6]

A rash that keeps spreading over several days should be looked at by your doctor, who can examine her skin directly.

Most diaper rash is not serious, but a rash that does not go away needs to be checked [6]. A pharmacist can recommend a diaper rash cream or medicine to treat it at home, such as a thin layer of a barrier cream at each diaper change [3].

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries in children are not serious, but any symptom needs medical help [2]. The usual symptoms after a knock to the head are headache, confusion, brief memory loss, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [1].

What you can do at home: keep an eye out for the symptoms listed below [6]. If he has a headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the dose your doctor indicates [6]. He can sleep, but after a more significant knock it is advisable to wake him every 4 hours [6]. No special diet is needed — he can eat as usual, according to his appetite [6]. Rest from physical and mental activity for 24 to 48 hours, with no sport and no screens, then a gradual return to normal activities [4].

Get help if:
- He was knocked out and has not woken up [2]
- He cannot stay awake or keep his eyes open [2]
- He has a fit (seizure) [2]
- Repeated vomiting [4]
- Confusion, or difficulty speaking or walking [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]

Most children recover quickly [6].

q: when can I start giving my baby solid foods
text:
Introducing solid foods, sometimes called complementary feeding or weaning, should start when your baby is around 6 months old, according to the NHS [2]. At first, how much they eat matters less than getting used to the idea of eating — they'll still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [2].

Start with a small amount of food before their usual milk feed, and don't worry about how much they eat [6]. Don't add sugar or salt to their food or cooking water [6]. Let them touch and hold the food, and allow them to feed themselves with their fingers as soon as they show an interest [6]. Keep trying new foods — it may take 10 tries or more for your baby to get used to them [6].

Food safety: always wash your hands and keep surfaces clean, wash and peel fruit and raw vegetables, remove pips, stones and bones, and cut small round foods like grapes into quarters [5]. Stay with your baby while they eat [5].

Talk to your pediatrician before starting solids if your baby was born prematurely [2], or before introducing nuts if there's a family history of allergies [3].

q: my 5 month old reaches for our food, can I start feeding him
text:
No, not yet — solid foods should start when your baby is around 6 months old, according to the NHS [2]. Reaching for your food is a sign of curiosity, but at 5 months his growth and nutrition still come from breast milk or first infant formula [1][2].

Until then, keep breastfeeding or formula feeding on demand. If you want to get him used to the idea, you can offer a few teaspoons of soft food once a day when he is around 6 months, before a milk feed, and let him set the pace [3]. Breast milk or formula stays his main drink through the first year, and whole cows' milk should not replace it before age 1 [3].

Ask your pediatrician when to start if your baby was born prematurely [2].

q: can I give peanut butter to my 6 month old
text:
Yes, you can give peanut butter to your 6-month-old, as long as it is served safely. According to the NHS, foods that can trigger allergies, including peanuts, can be introduced from around 6 months as part of your baby's diet, just like any other foods [1]. Serve peanut butter finely ground or as a nut butter — never whole nuts, which are a choking risk [1]. Introduce it one at a time so you can spot any reaction [1]. Once tolerated, keep it in your baby's usual diet to minimise the risk of allergy [1]. Delaying peanut beyond 6 to 12 months may increase the risk of developing an allergy to it [1].

If your baby already has a diagnosed food allergy or eczema, or you have a family history of food allergies, eczema, asthma or hay fever, talk to your doctor first [1].

Signs of an allergic reaction usually start between a few minutes and two hours after eating, and can include:

- Hives or red, itchy skin [3]
- Swelling of the face, tongue or lips [3]
- Vomiting or diarrhoea [3]
- Cough or wheezing [3]
- Trouble breathing, dizziness or fainting — this is an emergency [3]

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text:
Around 6 months, milk alone no longer meets your baby's energy and nutrient needs, so solid foods are needed alongside it, according to the WHO [1]. Start with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and build up the variety and texture of foods over time [1]. Aim for 2–3 meals a day at this age, plus breast milk or formula on demand [1].

The NHS says how much your baby eats at first matters less than getting used to eating — they still get most energy and nutrients from milk [2]. Offer one new food at a time so you can spot any allergic reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting, according to MedlinePlus [5].

Do not give honey before age 1, and avoid cow's milk and unpasteurised foods before 1 year [5]. Avoid choking risks like whole nuts, popcorn and whole grapes [5].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text:
For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and water comes mainly from food and milk rather than large amounts of plain water [2]. Offer water in a small cup with meals, but let them decide how much — the AEP says feeding should follow the child's hunger and fullness cues, not a set amount [2]. There is no fixed millilitre figure for water at this age in the guidance; the amount depends on the child [2].

What to do:
- Keep breastfeeding on demand, or offer the follow-on formula, as the main milk [2].
- Offer a little water in an open cup at mealtimes; let them stop when they are full [2].
- During illness, increase fluids, including more frequent breastfeeding [1].

Get help if:
- They drink much less than usual or have fewer wet nappies [1].
- They are drowsy, hard to wake, or breathing fast [1].
- They vomit repeatedly or have diarrhoea that will not stop [1].

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text:
It is common for babies and toddlers to prefer fruit and refuse vegetables, and it does not mean anything is wrong. The taste for different flavours, sweet, salty, sour and bitter, is built from an early age, and early exposure to different tastes may reduce the risk of refusing new foods, according to the AEP [3].

Keep offering a wide variety of fruits and vegetables, at any of the daily meals, and vary how you present them: puréed, mashed or in small pieces [3]. There are no better fruits than others to start with; it depends on the family's tastes [3]. Offer whole fruit rather than fruit juice, since juices offer no nutritional benefit over whole fruit and can displace other foods [3].

If your baby is under one year, avoid green leafy vegetables high in nitrates, such as chard, spinach or borage [3].

q: can a 7 month old eat eggs every day
text:
Yes, eggs can be part of a 7-month-old's diet every day. The AEP recommends offering protein-rich foods daily and in variety, including eggs, especially those rich in iron such as egg yolk [5]. It also advises introducing foods one at a time around 6 months, never before 4 months [3].

Offer them cooked and mashed or in small pieces, as part of a varied daily diet [5]. For iron, egg yolk is one good option among others like strips of cooked meat, lentil patties or tofu sticks [4].

Keep these safety rules at mealtimes:
- Baby sits upright, never lying down [4]
- Never leave a baby eating unsupervised [4]
- Avoid choking risks: whole nuts, popcorn, whole grapes, hard raw apple or carrot [4]

If you notice a reaction after eating eggs, such as swelling, hives or trouble breathing, get medical help.

text:
No — don't give honey to a baby under one year old. Honey can contain a toxin that causes botulism in infants, according to MedlinePlus [1].

Wait until your baby is 12 months old before offering any honey [1]. Until then, breast milk or infant formula covers their needs, and solid foods started around 6 months are fine [1][3].

Call your doctor if your baby has trouble feeding, seems very sleepy, is constipated, or has a weak cry — these can be signs of infant botulism.

text:
At 13 months, formula alone is not enough: from 6 months on, solid foods are needed alongside milk, according to the WHO [1]. Complementary feeding means giving solid or liquid foods in addition to formula, not instead of it [2].

Offer her solid foods several times a day, alongside her formula, and keep mealtimes calm and unhurried. The WHO notes that only about half of children aged 6 to 23 months get the number of meals they need each day [1].

Talk to your doctor or health visitor about how her growth and diet are going, especially if she is refusing solids or not gaining well.

q: how often should a newborn poop
text:
How often a newborn poops varies from baby to baby — the rhythm and consistency of stools differs from one person to another, according to the SEUP [3]. What matters more is the consistency: constipation is when stools become too hard, with discomfort or incomplete emptying, sometimes with fewer stools than usual [6].

For a baby under 6 months, keep feeding as usual with breast milk or formula [3]. Keep noting the baby's wet nappies and stools each day as part of their care [5].

Get help if:
- Baby is very floppy or crying a lot [3]
- Blood in the stool [3]
- Vomiting many times, not keeping down milk [3]
- Pain or crying with pooping [3]

Do not give any laxative or enema without asking your doctor [3].

q: my toddler has very hard poop and cries when he goes
text:
Hard, dry poop that hurts to pass is constipation, and in most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It means fewer than three bowel movements a week, and the stool can be hard and dry [3].

To help now: offer more water and other liquids, and more fruits, vegetables and grains, which are high in fiber [3]. The SEUP adds that the main thing is more fluids, preferably water, to soften the poop, and more meals with fiber — cereals and wholemeal bread, fruit, vegetables [1]. Do not replace fruit with juice, because juice has little fiber [1]. Laxatives only if your health care provider says so [3].

See your doctor if:
- Bad abdominal pain, or a child who is very down and complaining a lot [1]
- Blood in the stool [1]
- Vomiting many times, unable to keep down solids or liquids [1]
- Bowel habits change [3]

Most cases of childhood constipation (95%) are not caused by any illness [1].

q: what can I give my 2 year old for constipation
text:
Constipation is when poo becomes harder or less frequent, and most cases in children are not caused by any illness, according to the SEUP [3][1]. For a 2-year-old, the main things are more fluids, preferably water, and more fibre — cereals and wholegrain bread, fruit and vegetables; do not replace fruit with juice, as juice has little fibre [1]. Keep to a regular routine and don't let them hold in the urge to go [1]. Sitting on the toilet at the same time each day, best after a meal, for 5 to 10 minutes with feet supported, can help [6]. Do not give laxatives or enemas without asking your paediatrician [1]. See a doctor if:

- Bad tummy pain, or pain when pooing [1]
- Blood in the poo [1]
- Vomiting many times, keeping down neither food nor fluids [1]
- Very low energy and lots of complaining [1]

q: when can babies have cow's milk instead of formula
text:
No, cow's milk should not replace formula before 12 months. The AAP recommends all infants be fed breast milk or iron-fortified formula until at least 12 months of age, and does not recommend regular cow's milk for children under 1 year old [5]. Other milks, including cows' milk, should not be introduced as a main drink until 12 months of age, according to the NHS [4].

What to do now: keep giving breast milk or iron-fortified formula as the main drink. Formula-fed babies may need to eat about 6 to 8 times per day, and infant formula can be used until a child is 1 year old [5]. After 1 year, the child should only get whole milk, not skim or reduced-fat milk [5].

Talk with your baby's health care provider if you are unsure which formula is right, or if your baby is fussy — most of the time, cow's milk formulas are not the cause [1].

q: how much sleep should a 2 year old get
text:
For a 2-year-old, sleep needs are shown in the age table of the PUC Chile manual: children this age sleep about 11 to 14 hours in total, usually one afternoon nap plus the rest at night, and the nap continues until around age 4 [1][2].

What helps: keep the same bedtime and wake time every day, and always put them to sleep in their own bed [5]. Night waking is normal at this age — about 20 to 40% of children under 3 wake at night — and they should be left to settle back to sleep on their own, without your intervening, so a habit does not form [2]. If they fall asleep in your arms, they will want the same conditions to fall back asleep when they wake [2].

See your doctor if you are worried about their sleep, or if you feel you cannot cope — the PUC Chile manual notes that many sleep problems in young children improve with education and habits rather than medicine [4].

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text:
Night waking at this age is common and expected: by one year, about 30% of children wake at night, and 20–40% of children under three do, according to the PUC Chile manual [2]. Night wakings are physiological, and the same source says parents should not intervene, so the child learns to settle back to sleep on their own; a child who always falls asleep in your arms will look for those same conditions to fall back asleep [2].

What to do now: keep the bedtime routine calm and consistent, and give your baby the chance to resettle alone before going in [2]. If they have always been fed or held to sleep, expect the waking to continue until falling asleep happens in the cot instead [2].

See your doctor if your baby seems unwell, is not feeding or growing well, or the waking is accompanied by loud snoring or pauses in breathing [4][6].

q: my toddler snores every night but seems okay during the day
text:
Snoring at night with mouth breathing can be a sign of enlarged adenoids, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Children with enlarged adenoids often breathe through the mouth because the nose is blocked, mostly at night, and this may lead to bad breath, cracked lips, dry mouth, a persistent runny nose or nasal congestion [3]. Enlarged adenoids may also cause sleep problems: a child may be restless while sleeping, snore a lot, or have episodes of not breathing during sleep (sleep apnea) [3]. Children with enlarged adenoids may also have more frequent ear infections [3].

See your doctor if your child has episodes of not breathing during sleep, or frequent ear infections [3].

q: my 4 year old wakes up coughing only when he lies down
text:
A cough that comes on only when he lies down is one of the symptoms of asthma in children, according to MedlinePlus: coughing, especially at night or early in the morning, is common [5]. The SEUP also lists night-time cough among the symptoms of an asthma attack [3].

What to do now: keep a note of when the cough happens — at night, early morning, after running or playing, or after a cold — because that pattern helps your doctor [3][5]. There is nothing in these pages about a home remedy for a night cough, so do not give any medicine on your own.

Get medical help right away if:
- Severe coughing or serious trouble breathing [5]
- Turning very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [5]
- The chest pulls in and the ribs and collarbones show with each breath [3]
- Blue colour around the lips [3]
- Trouble speaking because of breathlessness [3]

See your doctor to have the cough looked at, since asthma symptoms can be mild or severe and come often or only now and then [5].

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text:
Using albuterol more often than usual can be a sign the asthma is not fully controlled, and the SEUP says most flare-ups are mild and can be treated at home with bronchodilators like salbutamol [3]. Give it with a spacer device — never straight into the mouth — because that helps the medicine reach the lungs [7]. If there is no clear improvement, the child needs to be seen at a health centre [7].

Get help urgently if:
- Very agitated or drowsy, or turning blue or pale [7]
- Breathing getting faster, ribs or chest pulling in, belly moving a lot [7]
- Needing inhalations every two hours or less [7]

The WHO notes that daily inhalers, including steroid ones, reduce the risk of severe attacks [2]. If your son needs his reliever this often, his treatment should be reviewed by your doctor.

q: he has an inhaler but I dont know when to use it
text:
A wheeze or cough from narrowed airways usually eases once a bronchodilator like salbutamol is given, according to the WHO [3]. Give it through a spacer, never straight into the mouth — it works better that way — and use a mask for small children [1][2]. Most flare-ups are mild and can be handled at home with the inhaler; symptoms usually settle in a few days, though they can last up to a week [2]. Keep him away from smoke and, during a flare-up, from exercise and allergens [2].

Get help if:
- He is very agitated or drowsy, or turns blue or pale [1]
- Breathing gets faster, ribs or chest pull in, belly moves a lot [1]
- He needs the inhaler every two hours or less [1]
- No clear improvement after using it [1]

If you go for care, bring the spacer with you [1].

text:
Fast breathing that settles with rest is often just the normal effect of running, but the SEUP says to watch for breathing difficulty — fast breathing, ribs pulling in, chest sinking, or tiring when walking or running [3]. If your daughter is otherwise well, she can keep up her usual activity [3].

What to do now: let her rest and watch her breathing while she is calm. If the fast breathing only happens with effort and goes back to normal at rest, that fits the pattern the SEUP describes as expected after exercise [3].

Get help today if:
- She seems generally unwell, drowsy, floppy or very irritable [3][4]
- Breathing difficulty appears or gets worse [3][4]
- Her ribs pull in, her chest sinks, or her tummy moves a lot with each breath [4]
- Chest or side pain when breathing [4]
- She refuses food and fluids repeatedly [4]

If you are worried about her breathing, contact your doctor [6].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be a sign of croup, an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe that often starts like a cold and causes noisy, harsh breathing [3]. Most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home, and symptoms usually get worse at night and last three to five days, according to MedlinePlus [3].

Keep her calm and comfortable, and offer fluids often. Croup is more common in children between six months and three years [3].

Get help if:
- Breathing becomes difficult or she seems to be struggling [3]
- She is drowsy, very irritable or not herself [1]
- The ribs pull in or the chest sinks with each breath [1][2]
- She cannot feed or drink [4]
- Her colour looks wrong [4]

If you are worried about her breathing, contact your doctor right away [3].

q: what are signs that a child is having trouble breathing
text:
Signs of trouble breathing include breathing problems such as shortness of breath, rapid breathing, or gasping for air, and wheezing — a whistling sound when breathing out — according to MedlinePlus [1]. You may also see the ribs pulling in, the chest sinking, or the belly moving with each breath [3][5].

Get medical help right away if your child has severe coughing, serious breathing problems, or turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [1]. Also seek urgent care if they are limp, sleepy or very irritable, have chest pain when breathing, or refuse food and fluids [5].

q: my son is hard to wake but he opens his eyes when I shake him

text:
A child who is hard to wake and only opens his eyes when shaken needs to be seen today — that is excessive drowsiness, and the SEUP lists "excessive drowsiness or problems waking your child" among the warning signs that mean going to the emergency department [1]. The WHO also lists difficulty waking in children as a sign of a serious problem needing immediate medical attention [4].

While you get him there: keep him lying on his side, do not give him anything to eat or drink, and do not leave him alone. If he has a fever, note it, and tell the staff how long he has been like this and whether he has vomited [1][4].

- Blue colour of face or lips [1]
- Trouble breathing or changed breathing [1]
- Very repeated vomiting [1]
- Fever above 38°C (100.4 °F) or shivering [1]
- Very irritable, or cannot stop crying [1]

q: my daughter is crying nonstop after a fall and wont calm down
text:
A head injury from a fall can cause headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness, according to the SEUP [1]. Your daughter's crying and inability to settle may be a sign that worries you, and the SEUP says to go to the emergency department if the child has any of the symptoms described or a behaviour or mood that concerns you [5].

Do not give her anything to eat or drink in case she needs tests, and do not let her play or use screens until she has been checked [6].

q: can a fever cause febrile seizures
banner: 🚨 Call 911 now or go to the emergency department. | Reason: Abnormal movements / seizure
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day.

A febrile seizure can sometimes happen when a child has a high temperature, according to the NHS [3]. It can seem frightening, but it is unlikely to harm your child or cause long-term effects [3]. They usually affect children between 6 months and 6 years old, and most last 2 to 3 minutes [4].

While the seizure is happening, keep your child safe: check the time it starts and ends, protect their head with your hands or something soft, and move dangerous objects away [6]. After it ends, put your child in the recovery position and make sure nothing is in their mouth or throat that might affect their breathing [6].

Get medical help if your child has a seizure for the first time, has one lasting more than 5 minutes, has trouble breathing, has stiffness or twitching on only one side, is more sleepy than usual for over an hour afterwards, or has more than one seizure within 24 hours [4].

q: my 4 year old had a seizure when he was a baby, does that change anything now
text:
A febrile seizure is a seizure that can happen when a child has a high temperature, and it is not usually serious or likely to cause long-term effects, according to the NHS [2]. Having had one does not mean your child has epilepsy; children who have had a febrile seizure have only a slightly increased chance of epilepsy later, and this is rare [3]. You cannot prevent febrile seizures [3].

If your child ever has another seizure:
- Note the time it starts and ends [4].
- Protect their head with your hands or something soft [4].
- Move dangerous objects away [4].
- After it ends, put them in the recovery position and check nothing is in their mouth or throat [4].
- Do not hold them still, put anything in their mouth, or try to cool them with cold water or by undressing them [1].

Get medical help if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, breathing is difficult, twitching is on one side only, they stay sleepier than usual for over an hour afterwards, or there is more than one seizure in 24 hours [5].

q: my child has a sore throat and white stuff on the tonsils
text:
A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils is often tonsillitis, a common childhood illness, according to the NHS [1]. The tonsils are red and swollen, and some children get pus-filled spots or white patches on them [1].

For comfort, have them drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, and rest [6]. Older children can gargle with warm salty water — half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water, then spit it out; young children should not try this [6]. Avoid smoky places [6]. A pharmacist can suggest treatments such as lozenges or throat sprays [2].

See a doctor if:
- Symptoms last more than 1 week [2]
- Repeated throat infections [2]
- Sore throat so painful they can't eat or drink [2]
- White pus-filled spots on the tonsils [2]

Get emergency help if:
- Severe sore throat that quickly gets worse [3]
- Swelling inside the mouth or throat [3]
- Difficulty speaking, swallowing or breathing [3]
- Difficulty opening the mouth [3]

q: when should I take my kid to the doctor for a sore throat
text:
A sore throat is very common and usually nothing to worry about — it normally gets better by itself within a week, according to the NHS [5]. Most are caused by viruses like a cold or flu [3].

To ease it: drink plenty of water, eat cool or soft foods, and rest [5]. Cool drinks, ice lollies or hard sweets can soothe it, but do not give young children anything small and hard to suck because of the risk of choking [5]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can help with the pain — ask a pharmacist about these [6]. Children should not take aspirin [1].

See a doctor if:
- Your child is under 5 and needs help for a sore throat [2]
- The sore throat does not improve after a week [2]
- A very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery [2]
- Signs of dehydration, such as peeing less than usual or dark, strong-smelling pee [2]

Get help immediately if your child has difficulty breathing or cannot swallow, is drooling, or makes a high-pitched sound when breathing [2].

q: my 5 year old has ear pain after having a cold
text:
Ear pain after a cold is often caused by a middle ear infection, which is common in young children and usually gets better on its own within about 3 days, according to the CDC [1][3].

For the pain, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours for the first 1 to 2 days, and it helps to give it regularly before the pain builds up, according to the SEUP [6]. Do not put anything in the ear to ease the pain, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [6]. If your child has little appetite, that is normal — do not force them to eat [6].

See a healthcare provider if:
- Fever of 102.2°F (39°C (102.2 °F)) or higher [7]
- Pus, discharge or fluid from the ear [7]
- Symptoms getting worse [7]
- Symptoms lasting more than 2–3 days [7]
- Hearing loss [7]

q: my 10 year old says he feels dizzy after playing outside in the heat
text:
Dizziness after playing outside in the heat can be a sign of heat exhaustion, which usually gets better if the child is cooled down within 30 minutes, according to the NHS [3].

Do this now: move him to a cool, shady place, take off extra clothing, and give him plenty of water to drink — an isotonic sports drink or oral rehydration powder mixed with water also helps replace salt lost through sweating [7]. Cool his skin by spraying or sponging him with cool water and fanning him; cold packs wrapped in a cloth under the armpits or on the neck work well too [7]. Stay with him until he feels better — he should start to cool down within 30 minutes [7].

Get help if:
- Still unwell after 30 minutes of cooling and fluids [7]
- Very high temperature, or hot red skin that is not sweating [7]
- Fast heartbeat or fast breathing [7]
- Confusion or lack of coordination [7]
- Seizure or loss of consciousness [7]

text:
A sunburn is damage to the outer layer of the skin caused by the sun, and it can be painful and cause swelling or blisters, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Keep your child out of the sun, offer plenty of fluids, and use a moisturising cream or after-sun lotion on the sore skin; antibiotic ointments can help prevent infection if the skin is broken [2]. - The burn covers a large area or looks deep [2]
- There are blisters, swelling or signs of infection [2]

Jaundice at around 3 days old is common in babies, and for most it is harmless and gets better without treatment, according to the NHS [1]. The yellowing usually starts on the face and spreads, and is often most noticeable at about 3 days old; it usually takes around 2 weeks to go [1].

Because your baby is under 3 months, they need to be seen by a doctor today. Keep feeding them as usual, and keep a nappy with pale poo or dark urine to show the doctor if you notice it [1].

Get help now if your baby:
- is sleepier than normal or hard to wake [1]
- is not feeding [1]
- is floppy or stiff, or has jerking or twitching movements [1]
- has a temperature of 38C (100.4 °F) or more, or 36C (96.8 °F) or less, or feels hot or cold [1]
- has no wet nappies, or is breathing fast or with grunting [1]

It is common for newborns to wake often to feed, and a baby who is feeding less than before needs to be checked. A healthy newborn should be assessed for poor feeding, lethargy and poor sucking, according to the AEP [1]. - Lethargy or unusual sleepiness [1]
- Irritability [1]
- Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes) [1]
- Breathing difficulty or bluish colour [1]

A newborn this young should be seen by a paediatrician within 24 to 48 hours of leaving hospital, and then at least weekly until feeding is established with good weight gain, according to SENeo [2].

text:
A 4-month-old should be wetting nappies frequently, with clear, odourless urine — especially if they are breastfed only, according to the Junta de Andalucía [6]. The number of wet nappies varies a lot from baby to baby, so what matters is that they keep wetting them often [6].

q: can babies get dehydrated from breastfeeding
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, little urine, dry mouth, persistent vomiting or heavy diarrhoea >24 h
text:
Yes, babies can get dehydrated, and breastfeeding is one of the best protections against it. Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in [1]. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months helps prevent it, according to the WHO [5].

Keep breastfeeding normally, and even more often if your baby wants it — breast milk is exactly what they need, and it should continue during episodes of diarrhoea or vomiting [3][5]. If your baby is also vomiting, wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution, 2–5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, according to the SEUP [6]. Watch how well they take it; if fluids stay down, you can slowly increase how often you offer them [6].

Get help if you notice:
- Sunken eyes, dry mouth, or very little urine [1]
- Vomiting a lot, or not keeping down solids or liquids [3]
- Green vomit, blood, or brown coffee-ground material [3]
- Persistent diarrhoea, blood in the stool, or signs of dehydration [5]

The HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus (HPV), a common virus spread by skin contact, usually during sex. Some types of HPV are linked to cancers including cervical, mouth, anal, penile, vulval and vaginal cancer, and to genital warts, according to the NHS [1].

It works very well: since it has been used there has been a big drop in young people getting conditions linked to HPV, such as cervical cancer and genital warts [2]. In the United States the ages for this vaccine follow the national schedule, so ask your doctor when your daughter is due.

The most common side effects are mild and do not last long: swelling or pain where the injection was given, headache, a high temperature, dizziness, feeling sick, tiredness [5]. A severe allergic reaction is very rare, and the person who vaccinates is trained to treat it immediately [5].

Get help if:
- swelling or pain at the injection site that worries you [5]
- a high temperature [5]
- dizziness, feeling sick or unusual tiredness [5]

Common side effects are usually mild and last only 2 to 3 days: a raised, blotchy rash, feeling unwell, and a high temperature around 7 to 11 days after the vaccination; swollen glands around the cheeks, neck and jaw and aching joints around 2 to 3 weeks after [5].

Get help if:
- A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) — rare, and the person who vaccinates is trained to treat it immediately [5].

The ages for each dose follow the United States's national schedule, so check the timing with your doctor.

q: I read that vaccines can cause autism, is that actually true
text:
No, that is not true: many scientific studies have looked at this and found no link between vaccines and autism, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Vaccines are safe, and they must go through extensive safety testing and evaluation before they are approved in the United States [1].

If you are wondering when your child should be vaccinated, they get their vaccines at well-child visits, following the vaccination schedule [4]. That schedule lists the recommended vaccines, who should get them, how many doses they need and at what age, and the CDC publishes it for the United States [4]. Following it lets your child build immunity before being exposed to very serious diseases [4].

q: my son missed his 4 month vaccines, what do we do now
text:
For a missed 4-month visit, the usual approach is to give the vaccines now rather than restart the schedule, according to the AEP [1][5]. The same vaccine doses are used as for any other baby, and there is no reason to give a reduced or split dose [1][5]. Between doses of the same vaccine, an interval of at least 4 weeks is generally needed, depending on the vaccine [5].

Your doctor or clinic can tell you exactly which vaccines your son needs and when to bring him in, following the United States national schedule.

q: does the flu shot give children the flu
text:
No, the flu shot cannot give your child the flu. The shot is made with inactivated or recombinant virus, so it does not contain live flu virus [6]. The nasal spray vaccine does contain live weakened virus, but it is approved only for people 2 through 49 years old and is not recommended for pregnant women or people with certain underlying medical conditions [2].

The CDC recommends a flu vaccine every year for everyone 6 months and older, using any licensed, age-appropriate vaccine [2]. The flu vaccine is the best way to prevent flu, and it is given annually because protection fades over time [5].

That spotty rash may contain infectious chickenpox virus, so keep it covered with clothes; as long as the spots are covered, children can go to nursery as normal [2].

What can help: drink plenty of water, get plenty of rest, and try to relax, since stress can make headaches worse [5]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken for the pain [5]. - Headache is very intense, getting worse, or not responding to usual treatment [2]

Get help if:
- Not able to drink or breastfeed [1]
- Vomits everything [1]
- Convulsions or fits [1]
- Lethargic or unconscious [1]
- Stiff neck [1]

Also watch their general state and colour, and for red spots that do not fade when pressed [5].

q: my child has asthma but is not wheezing right now, should I still use albuterol
text:
The sources describe asthma as a chronic condition whose symptoms come and go, and they do not say to give a reliever inhaler when there are no symptoms at all [2][4]. The SEUP guidance on asthma attacks is about treating an attack that is happening — cough, trouble breathing, chest noises — and it says salbutamol is given then, 2 to 4 puffs one at a time through a spacer, repeated after 10 to 15 minutes [1][6]. If your child has no cough, no chest tightness and no breathing trouble right now, there is nothing in these passages that tells you to use albuterol now.

Get help if:
- Very agitated or drowsy, or turning blue or pale [7]
- Breathing getting faster, ribs or chest pulling in [7]
- Needing inhalations every two hours or less [7]
- No clear improvement after treatment at home [6]

Keep your child's maintenance treatment going during an attack, and keep them away from tobacco smoke [5][6]. If you are unsure, your doctor can go over your child's asthma action plan with you.

q: I found a lump behind my baby's ear, should I worry
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Swelling or redness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward: it should be seen today
text:
A lump behind the ear is not one of the usual signs of an ear infection. Ear infections are very common in children and often get better on their own within 3 days, according to the NHS [2]. The usual signs are pain inside the ear, a high temperature, difficulty hearing, discharge from the ear, or a feeling of pressure or fullness [2]. Babies may rub or pull their ear, be irritable or restless, be off their food, or keep losing their balance [2].

While you are getting your baby seen, you can treat any ear pain: give ibuprofen or paracetamol every 6 to 8 hours regularly for the first 1 to 2 days, according to the SEUP [3]. Do not put anything in the ear to calm the pain, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has discharged [3]. If your baby is a young infant, do frequent nasal washes with saline [3]. It is normal for them to have little appetite, so do not force them to eat [3].

Get help today if there is redness, pain or swelling behind the ear, or the ear is pushed forward [5].

q: my toddler has a swollen eyelid after waking up
text:
A swollen eyelid in a toddler can be a sign of roseola, a common infection that usually causes a high temperature and a rash, according to the NHS [3]. Along with the swollen eyelids, your child may have cold-like symptoms such as a sore throat, runny nose and cough, and may lose their appetite [3]. These symptoms usually last 3 to 5 days, and then a rash of pinkish-red spots appears, starting on the chest, tummy and back before spreading to the face, neck and arms [3]. The rash normally fades within 2 days [3].

You can normally look after your child at home, and they should recover within a week [3].

Get help if:
- Your child has trouble breathing [5]
- Their lips look blue, or they are drooling [5]
- They are pale [5]
- They lose consciousness [5]

q: my child has a headache after looking at a screen for hours
text:
Most headaches go away on their own and are not a sign of something more serious, according to the NHS [2]. A headache after long screen use is one of the things the NHS says to avoid, so cutting down screen time can help [1].

What to do now: have them drink plenty of water and get some rest [2]. Try to relax, since stress can make headaches worse [2]. The SEUP advises reducing screen use as much as possible, keeping a calm environment, and making sure they get enough sleep [4]. A usual painkiller such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen and rest usually ease it [5].

- It wakes them at night [3]
- They are much sleepier than usual or hard to wake [3]
- Repeated vomiting with a severe headache [3]
- Vision, walking, arm or leg movement, or speech problems [3]

q: my 5 year old complains that his stomach hurts before he poops
text:
Stomach pain just before pooing is a common symptom of constipation, according to the SEUP: the stools become harder and more painful to pass, and this can cause tummy pain, bloating and a feeling of not having finished [2][3]. Most cases of childhood constipation (95%) are not caused by any illness [1].

What helps: offer more fluids, preferably water, to soften the stools, and more fibre — wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit and vegetables. Do not replace fruit with juice, which has little fibre [1]. Keep to a regular routine and don't let him hold in the urge to go to the toilet [1]. Don't give laxatives or enemas without asking your paediatrician [1].

See a doctor if:
- Severe tummy pain, or he seems very unwell and complains a lot [1]
- Blood in the stools [1]
- Vomiting many times, unable to keep down solids or fluids [1]
- Pain on passing stool, or anal fissures [2][3]

q: my daughter has stomach pain and hasnt pooped in three days
text:
It sounds like constipation: not having a poo at least 3 times in the last week, or pooing less often than usual, with poo that is dry, hard or lumpy, and straining or pain when passing it [1]. Stomach ache and feeling bloated or sick can come with it [1]. In most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious [2].

What helps: offer more fluids, preferably water, to soften the poo and make it easier to pass [3]. Add more fibre — wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit and vegetables [3]. Don't replace fruit with juice, which has little fibre [3]. Don't give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

Get help if:
- Bad stomach pain, or they seem very unwell and complain a lot [3]
- Blood in the poo [3]
- Vomiting many times, can't keep down solids or liquids [3]
- Pain when passing a poo [3]

It's not essential to poo every day; the rhythm varies from child to child [3].

q: my son has diarrhea but wants to eat normally
text:
It is usually fine for a child with diarrhea to keep eating, and the main treatment is replacing lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration [4]. Give your son an oral rehydration solution to replace the fluids and electrolytes he is losing [4]. As his symptoms improve, he can eat soft, bland food [4]. Gastroenteritis usually gets better on its own with rest and plenty of fluids and electrolytes, according to MedlinePlus [1].

Contact a provider right away if he has any of these, according to MedlinePlus [2]:
- Diarrhea lasting more than a day
- Change in mental state, such as irritability or lack of energy
- Signs of dehydration, such as thirst, dry mouth, urinating less than usual or no wet diapers for 3 hours or more, and no tears when crying
- Frequent loose stools or vomiting often
- Severe pain in the abdomen or rectum, or stools that are black and tarry or contain blood or pus

q: my baby vomited once after drinking a full bottle very fast
text:
A single vomit after a fast bottle is usually just that — the feed came back up — and it is not the same as the vomiting illness the guidance describes [1]. Carry on feeding: keep breastfeeding or using formula, and if your baby is being sick, give smaller feeds more often than usual [1][4]. If your baby is on formula or solid foods, offer small sips of water between feeds — for a baby under 6 months, boil the water first and let it cool [1][4]. Do not make formula weaker, and do not give fruit juice or fizzy drinks [4].

Get help if:
- Your baby is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [3]
- Vomiting is repeated, or they cannot keep down solids or liquids [3]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [3]
- They are sleepy, floppy, very thirsty, have sunken eyes, cry without tears, or pass little urine [3]
- There is severe tummy pain or a headache [3]

q: my 2 year old vomited during the night and is fine this morning
text:
A single vomit during the night, with your child well the next morning, is not usually a cause for concern. The main risk with vomiting is dehydration, according to the SEUP [3].

Offer fluids often in small amounts, using an oral rehydration solution [3]. Keep giving their normal food in smaller, more frequent portions, and don't force them to eat [4]. Avoid fatty foods, sweets and juices, and skip sports drinks [4]. You can keep breastfeeding as usual, or more often if they want it [4].

Get help if:
- Vomiting a lot, can't keep down solids or fluids, or vomits even without drinking [2][4]
- Green vomit, blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds [2][4]
- Drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [2]
- Severe tummy pain or headache [2]

q: my child has a fever but his hands are freezing cold
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Cold hands and feet in a child with fever: it may be poor circulation, get it checked
text:
If your child is under 3 months old, a fever needs a doctor the same day. For an older child, cold hands and feet with a fever are common: the body sends blood inward to raise its temperature, so the skin feels cold, according to the SEUP [7].

What to do now: check the temperature with a thermometer, preferably under the arm [5]. If there are no warning signs, start with physical measures — take off extra clothing, offer plenty of fluids, reduce activity, and a lukewarm bath only if the child is comfortable [5]. Do not undress or sponge the child to cool them, and do not wrap them in too many clothes or blankets [2]. If the child is uncomfortable with a fever above 38°C (100.4 °F), give the antipyretic your paediatrician usually recommends; the dose depends on age and weight [6]. Do not give aspirin to a child under 16 [2].

Get help if:
- Drowsy, not reacting, or very irritable [1]
- Trouble breathing [1]
- Spots that do not fade when pressed [1]
- Will not take solids or liquids [1]
- Under 2 months old or immune-depressed [1]

q: she feels hot but the thermometer says 98.6
text:
A temperature of 98.6°F (37°C (98.6 °F)) is normal, not a fever — a fever is 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, according to the NHS [1]. Feeling hot to the touch on its own does not mean a fever; a digital thermometer reading is what counts [1].

If your child does have a fever, the goal is their comfort, not bringing the number down, according to the SEUP [3]. Keep them well hydrated, in a neutral, ventilated room, and avoid over-wrapping them [3]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease the discomfort, at the dose your paediatrician recommends, every 6–8 hours [3]. Do not alternate them routinely every 3–4 hours [3]. Do not bathe them in cold water or use wet cloths — it is unpleasant and does not work [3]. It is normal for them to have less appetite; do not force food, but offer plenty of fluids [3].

Get help if your child:
- has a rash that does not fade when pressed [4][7]
- is drowsy and hard to wake, or confused [7]
- has difficulty breathing [7]
- has a stiff neck or is bothered by light [7]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [7]

If your baby is under 3 months old, a temperature this high needs a doctor the same day. For an older baby, a fever is the body fighting an infection, and most often it is caused by a common viral illness, according to the SEUP [4].

You can give either paracetamol or ibuprofen if your baby is distressed or uncomfortable; check the leaflet to be sure the medicine suits your child, and the dose depends on their age and weight [2].

- Confusion that is getting worse, or agitation
- Repeated vomiting
- A headache that gets worse or does not go away
- Trouble speaking, or weakness or numbness in the arms or legs

q: she hit her head last week and has been completely normal until today
text:
Most head injuries are not serious, but it's important to get medical help for any symptoms, according to the NHS [3]. A concussion can last a few weeks [3].

If there is headache, you can give ibuprofen or paracetamol in the doses indicated by your doctor, according to the SEUP [5]. They can sleep, but after a more significant injury it is advisable to wake them every 4 hours [5]. Keep them resting physically and mentally for 24 to 48 hours, with no sports or screens, then return to normal activities gradually [2]. Eating normally is fine [5].

Get urgent medical help if, after a head injury, they:
- cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open [3]
- have a seizure [3]
- have problems with vision, hearing, walking, balance, speaking or understanding [3]
- have clear fluid or blood from the ears or nose [3]
- have new numbness or weakness [3]

See a doctor if symptoms last more than 2 weeks [6].

q: my child says he feels like he cant catch his breath but his oxygen monitor says 99
text:
A child who says he cannot catch his breath needs to be checked, even when the monitor reads 99. Difficulty breathing is one of the signs the SEUP says to watch for at home, and it is a reason to go to the emergency department [2]. The SEUP also lists difficulty breathing as a reason to seek urgent care in bronchiolitis and pneumonia [3][5].

While you get him seen, keep him calm and sitting upright, and do not leave him alone.

Signs that make it more serious, according to the SEUP:
- Breathing fast, ribs pulling in or chest sinking [2][3]
- Very drowsy, floppy or very irritable [2][5]
- Chest pain when breathing [2][5]
- Poor colour [5]
- Refusing food and fluids [5]

If you are worried about your child's breathing, call your doctor straight away, as MedlinePlus advises for croup [4].

text:
Fast breathing that comes with crying is expected, and it usually settles once the crying stops. Fast breathing is a sign of breathing difficulty when it happens at rest, along with ribs pulling in or the chest dipping, according to the SEUP [3][4].

If your daughter is calm and breathing comfortably now, she can stay home and rest; there is no need to wake her or hold her upright. If she has a cold or a cough, keep her nose clear and offer fluids often [3].

- Refusing feeds and fluids [4]

q: he has a cough and is breathing normally when asleep
text:
A cough with normal breathing during sleep is usually a mild cold or similar infection, and most cases can be managed at home [1][5]. Keep offering fluids and let him rest; there is no medicine that cures these viral coughs, and most improve over about two weeks, though the cough can last longer [5].

Watch at home for signs he is getting worse:
- Breathing faster, ribs pulling in, or chest sinking [1][3]
- Tiredness or struggling to feed or drink [3][5]
- Chest pain when breathing [1]
- Becoming drowsy, floppy or very irritable [1]
- Fever that concerns you [5]

text:
Some babies sleep much more than others, and all babies change their sleep patterns as they grow — growth spurts, teething and illnesses can all affect how a baby sleeps, according to the NHS [1][2]. Waking up and drinking normally is a good sign.

If you want more advice about your baby's sleep or getting into a routine, speak to your pediatrician [2].

q: my child has a rash after taking amoxicillin, is it an allergy

A rash is the most common type of drug reaction, and medicines are one of the usual causes of hives, according to MedlinePlus [5][3]. Hives are raised, reddish, sometimes itchy patches that often go away on their own, though a serious case may need medicine or an injection [3].

q: my son has a small cut from a rusty nail
text:
A small cut from a rusty nail is a wound that tetanus spores can infect, according to the WHO [5]. Tetanus is preventable with vaccination, and most cases are linked to wounds like this one [5].

Clean the wound thoroughly and check that your son's tetanus vaccinations are up to date — the vaccine is what prevents tetanus after a cut or wound [5]. If he is not fully vaccinated, or you are unsure, contact your doctor so they can advise on vaccination [5].

- Sudden painful spasms, sometimes set off by sudden noise [6]
- Trouble swallowing [6]
- Seizures [6]

Red cheeks can be an early sign that a baby has a high temperature, according to the NHS [2]. A high temperature in babies is usually 38C (100.4 °F) or above, and a normal temperature is about 36.4C (97.5 °F) [2].

Check your baby's temperature with a digital thermometer — it is the most accurate way for a baby or young child [2][7]. If your baby feels hotter than usual on their back or chest, feels sweaty or clammy, or has flushed cheeks, that can suggest a high temperature [2].

Get medical advice if:
- Your baby is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38C (100.4 °F) or above [2]
- Your baby is 3 to 6 months and has a temperature of 39C (102.2 °F) or above [2]
- Your baby has other signs of illness, such as poor feeding, irritability or reduced wet nappies [2]
- You are worried about your baby [2]

Do not use an old-fashioned glass thermometer containing mercury — it can break and release poisonous mercury [7].

q: my child has chickenpox, when can he go back to school
text:
Chickenpox is very contagious, and children usually miss 5 to 6 days of school or childcare because of it, according to the CDC [1]. A person with chickenpox is contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash begins until all the lesions have crusted over [2]. It usually takes about a week for all the blisters to become scabs [3].

So he can go back to school once all the spots have scabbed over and no new ones are appearing [2]. If he was vaccinated and gets chickenpox, the spots may not crust, and he is contagious until no new lesions have appeared for 24 hours [2].

Keep him away from anyone who is pregnant or has a weakened immune system while he is still contagious [2].

q: my 2 year old weighs 40 pounds, should I be worried
text:
40 lb = 18.1 kg.

It is not possible to say from weight alone whether a 2-year-old is in the healthy range: weight has to be looked at together with height, according to the NHS [1]. Once a child is 2, their weight and height can be used to work out their body mass index and plot it on a centile chart, which is how you check whether their weight is in the healthy range [1]. If they are overweight or underweight, you can get advice about their diet and physical activity levels [1].

For children under 5, the WHO defines overweight as a weight-for-height more than 2 standard deviations above the median of its growth standards, and obesity as more than 3 standard deviations above [6]. The WHO also advises avoiding restrictive diets in young children who are still growing [2].

So the useful next step is to have your child's weight and height measured and plotted on a growth chart, and to talk to your doctor or pediatrician about the result [1].

Note: 18.1 kg is very high for a child of 2 years on the WHO growth charts. If it was a typo, correct it, because doses go by weight; if it is right, mention it to your doctor.

q: my baby was born early and I am not sure when to start solids
text:
Around 6 months is when solid foods usually start, according to the NHS [1]. If your baby was born prematurely, ask your baby's doctor for advice on when to start [1].

At the beginning, how much your baby eats matters less than getting used to eating — they still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [1]. Start with single vegetables and fruits, mashed or as soft cooked sticks, and include ones that are not sweet, like broccoli, cauliflower and spinach [5]. Let cooked food cool right down before offering it [5]. You can introduce foods containing allergens — peanuts, eggs, gluten, fish — from around 6 months, one at a time and in small amounts, so you can spot any reaction [5]. Cows' milk can be used in cooking or mixed with food from around 6 months, but not as a main drink until 1 year [5]. Babies do not need salt or sugar added to their food or cooking water [5].

Whether you spoon-feed, let your baby feed themselves finger foods, or do both, there is no right or wrong way [2].

q: my 9 month old still has no teeth, is that normal
text:
It is normal for a 9-month-old not to have teeth yet. A first tooth usually appears between 4 and 8 months, but some babies are later, according to MedlinePlus [4].

Until then, wipe the gums with a damp washcloth after each meal [4]. Do not put your baby to bed with a bottle of milk, juice or sugar water — use only water for bedtime bottles [4]. As soon as the first tooth shows, switch to a soft toothbrush [4]. Ask your health care provider whether your baby needs oral fluoride [4].

Once teeth come in, brush them at least twice a day, especially before bed, and do the real brushing yourself [1]. Take your child to a dentist every 6 months [1].

Get help immediately if:
- Lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell [7]
- Breathing is very fast or struggling [7]

- Skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale [7]
- Sudden confusion, drowsiness or dizziness, or fainting [7]

q: my child has been bitten by mosquitoes while visiting Nigeria
text:
Mosquito bites usually just itch, but mosquitoes in some parts of the world can spread malaria, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Because your child was bitten in Nigeria, malaria is a real concern: it can cause high fevers, shaking chills, flu-like symptoms and anaemia, and children under 5 account for most malaria deaths in that region, the WHO says [3][6].

What to do now: see a doctor about your child, since malaria is serious and needs to be checked. If you are still travelling or planning to, the WHO advises talking to a doctor about preventive medicines before travel to malaria areas [3]. To prevent further bites, use mosquito repellent (DEET, IR3535 or Icaridin) after dusk, sleep under a mosquito net, wear long sleeves and trousers at dusk, and use window screens [3][4].

Get help urgently if your child has:
- a high fever or shaking chills [6]
- flu-like symptoms [6]
- unusual tiredness or looking pale (anaemia) [6]
- symptoms that get worse or are not getting better [5]
- swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing [5]

q: my son has had a dry cough for three weeks
text:
A dry cough lasting three weeks or more is a reason to have your son examined for tuberculosis, according to the Ministério da Saúde [1]. The main symptom of pulmonary tuberculosis is cough, which may be dry or productive, and anyone with respiratory symptoms such as cough for three weeks or more should be evaluated [1]. Other symptoms can include afternoon fever, night sweats and weight loss [1]. Take him to a health unit for assessment and testing [1]. If the result is positive, treatment should start as soon as possible and be followed to the end [1].

Because he is under 3 months old, do not give any cough or cold medicine at home — talk to your child's health professional before giving any medicine for cough or cold [5].

Get help if:
- Trouble breathing or fast breathing [5]
- Fever lasting more than 4 days [5]
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement [5]
- Symptoms that improve then return or worsen [5]

A single swallowed magnet usually causes no problems, but swallowing several magnetic pieces can cause the bowel to twist, according to the SEUP [6]. q: my toddler has diarrhoea since yesterday, can I give him milk

Diarrhoea in a toddler is usually not serious and gets better on its own, according to MedlinePlus [1]. Yes, you can keep giving milk: it is not necessary to avoid dairy products, and you can keep breastfeeding normally, even more often if he asks for it [6].

What to do now: keep him drinking. Offer an oral rehydration solution in small amounts, more often than usual, and let him eat a practically normal diet in smaller portions — no need to fast [6]. - Frequent loose stools or vomiting often [2]
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, no tears when crying [2]
- Blood or pus in the stools, or black tarry stools [2]

q: my daughter has a barking cough but seems okay between coughs
text:
A barking cough that sounds like a seal, with a hoarse voice, is usually croup — an inflammation of the vocal cords and windpipe that is most often caused by a virus, according to MedlinePlus [3]. Most cases of viral croup are mild and can be treated at home [3].

Keep your daughter calm and comfortable, since the cough can get worse when a child is upset or crying [5]. Offer fluids, and if she has a fever you can give the usual fever medicine [6]. Symptoms are often worse at night and usually settle within a few days, though they can last up to a week [6].

Get help if:
- Breathing becomes difficult or noisy [4][6]
- She turns pale or unwell-looking, or her general condition worsens [6]
- The cough is getting worse or she is not getting better [4]
- She is under 3 months old [4]

If you are worried about her breathing, contact your doctor right away [3].

Itchy red patches on the skin are a common symptom of eczema, which is not contagious, according to MedlinePlus [2]. Scratching can make the skin redder and the itch worse [2].

q: my son has been constipated since we started weaning
text:
Constipation means fewer than three bowel movements a week, and the stool can be hard, dry and painful to pass; in most cases it lasts a short time and is not serious, according to MedlinePlus [2]. It is not important that he has a bowel movement every day, but if his bowel habits have changed, check with your doctor [2].

What usually helps, according to the SEUP: offer more fluids, preferably water, to soften the stool; add more fibre-rich meals (fibre cereals and bread, fruit, vegetables); and do not replace fruit with juices, which have little fibre [3]. Most childhood constipation (95%) is not caused by any disease, and you should not give laxatives or enemas without asking your paediatrician [3].

See your doctor if:
- Tummy pain that is severe, or he is very down and complaining a lot [3]
- Blood in the stool [3]
- Vomiting many times, unable to keep down solids or liquids [3]
- Constipation not getting better with treatment, or he is regularly constipated or bloated [1]

q: when can I start weaning my baby
text:
Introducing solid foods, sometimes called weaning, should start when your baby is around 6 months old, according to the NHS [3]. At the beginning, how much they eat matters less than getting used to the idea of eating — they'll still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [3].

If your baby was born prematurely, ask your health visitor or GP for advice on when to start [3].

You can give nuts from the time you start weaning, as long as they're crushed or ground and added to food, or as nut butter spread onto food like toast — never on its own, as it could choke them [2]. Whole nuts should not be given to children under 5 [2]. If there's a history of food allergies in your family, talk to your GP or health visitor before introducing any type of nut [2].

q: my child has chickenpox, when can she go back to nursery
text:
Chickenpox is very contagious, and children usually miss 5 to 6 days of school or childcare because of it, according to the CDC [2]. Your child can go back once all the spots have formed a scab — usually 5 days after the spots first appeared, the NHS says [5].

While she is at home: give her plenty of fluids (ice lollies help if she will not drink), paracetamol for pain and discomfort, and keep her fingernails cut with socks on her hands at night so she does not scratch [5]. Cool baths, loose clothes and cooling creams or gels from a pharmacy can ease the itching; ask a pharmacist about antihistamine medicine [5]. Do not give ibuprofen unless a doctor tells you to, and never aspirin to a child under 16 [5].

Keep her away from newborn babies, anyone pregnant, and anyone with a weakened immune system, as chickenpox can be dangerous for them [5].

text:
Signs of dehydration include being very thirsty, crying without tears, passing little urine, or sunken eyes, according to the SEUP [2]. q: can I give ORS to my 1 year old after diarrhea
text:
Yes, you can give oral rehydration salts (ORS) to your 1-year-old after diarrhoea. The WHO lists rehydration with ORS as a key treatment for diarrhoea, and ORS is a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar that replaces the water and electrolytes lost in the stools [1]. The WHO also lists zinc supplements as a key treatment: they reduce how long the diarrhoea lasts by 25% and the stool volume by 30% [1]. Keep giving nutrient-rich foods, including breast milk, during the episode [1].

- Much thirst, crying without tears, little urine or sunken eyes [3]
- Marked irritability, drowsiness or reduced responsiveness [3]
- Stools so watery and frequent that the child cannot drink fast enough [3]
- Refusing to eat or drink [3]

q: my 5 year old has stomach pain and constipation
text:
Stomach pain with constipation is common in children, and most causes are mild and get better on their own, according to the SEUP [2]. Constipation is likely if your child has not pooed at least 3 times in the last week, or the poo is large, dry, hard or lumpy, or they strain or feel pain when they poo [1].

What helps: offer more fluids, preferably water, to soften the poo; give more fibre (wholegrain cereals and bread, fruit, vegetables); and do not replace fruit with juice, as juice has little fibre [3]. Keep a regular routine and don't let them hold in the urge to go [3]. Don't give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

Get help if:
- Severe tummy pain, or a child who is very down and complaining a lot [3]
- Blood in the poo [3]
- Vomiting many times, unable to keep down food or drink [3]
- Intense, continuous pain or generally unwell [4]

Most childhood constipation (95%) is not caused by any disease [3].

q: when should I start solids for my baby
text:
Introducing solid foods should start when your baby is around 6 months old, according to the NHS [2]. At the beginning, how much your baby eats matters less than getting them used to the idea of eating — they'll still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [2].

It's good to wait until around 6 months because breast milk or first infant formula gives your baby what they need until then, and waiting gives them time to develop so they can cope with solid foods — moving food around their mouth, chewing and swallowing [4]. If your baby was born prematurely, ask your doctor for advice on when to start [2].

You can offer finger foods and let your baby feed themselves, or feed purées and mashed food on a spoon, or a mix of both — there's no right or wrong way [1]. What matters most is that your baby eats a wide variety of food and gets the nutrients they need [1].
